pull request.plain: a proposed change to the product, set aside for checking before it joins the real thing
pull request.example: Like a draft of a page you hand to an editor: nothing is printed until the editor agrees.

CI.plain: the automatic checks that run on every change
CI.example: Like the safety inspection a car goes through before it leaves the factory.

merge.plain: to join a checked change into the real product
merge.example: Like adding the edited page into the finished book.

branch.plain: a separate copy of the work where a change is made without touching the real product
branch.example: Like photocopying a recipe so you can try a new spice without spoiling the original.

commit.plain: one saved step of the work, with a short note on what changed
commit.example: Like a numbered save point in a game: you can always go back to it.

review.plain: a second, independent agent reading a change closely and signing off that it is clean; no change joins the product without one
review.example: Like a proofreader who must initial the page before it is printed.

slice.plain: one finished piece of a bigger feature, sent up as its own pull request and kept hidden behind a feature flag until you switch it on
slice.example: Like building a house room by room, with each room inspected before the next.

lane.plain: how much process a piece of work goes through (quick, small, feature or bug); the bigger the lane, the more planning and checking
lane.example: Like the express and full-service checkouts at a shop.

feature flag.plain: a switch that keeps finished work hidden from users until you decide to turn it on
feature flag.example: Like a curtain over a new shop window until opening day.

preview.plain: a private copy of the product with the change in it, so you can look before it goes live
preview.example: Like a rehearsal performance before opening night.

worktree.plain: a separate working folder where one agent builds one piece of work without getting in the way of the others
worktree.example: Like giving each builder their own workbench.

STOP.plain: the big red button: every agent stops until you lift it
STOP.example: Like pulling the emergency cord on a train.

Standard.plain: the normal protection level, and the default: it guards against agents' mistakes and against being misled by what they read, and asks nothing extra of you
Standard.example: Like an ordinary door lock: it keeps out the wrong turn and the casual try, but not someone set on getting in.

Locked.plain: the optional stronger protection level, set up once with your computer's password: it stops an agent getting round the safety checks even if it tries, because the checks sit where only an administrator can change them
Locked.example: Like adding a deadbolt and an alarm to that door. Who signs things off stays the same; what changes is how hard the checks are to get round.

the helper.plain: a small program on your computer, outside the agents' sandbox, that alone holds the keys to your code host and the signing key; agents can only ask it to act, and its checks apply to every request
the helper.phrase: the key-holding program on your computer
the helper.example: Like a bank teller who handles the money so the clerks never touch the vault.

the foreman.plain: the agent that runs a project's building: it queues work, writes briefs, starts and closes the builder sessions, checks for clashes, passes questions to you and merges through the gate, but never builds
the foreman.phrase: the agent that runs the building
the foreman.example: Like the site manager on a building job, who is not laying bricks but knows who is.

the gate.plain: the last checks a change must pass at the moment it merges: tests green on exactly that version, a clean signed review, and still fitting with the latest product
the gate.phrase: the final check before a change joins the product
the gate.example: Like passport control: nobody walks through without being checked.

appetite.plain: how much effort a piece of work is worth, set when you approve it; if the work runs past it, it pauses and comes back to you with what was learnt
appetite.example: Like deciding a weekend job is worth a weekend, and stopping to ask if it is heading for a month.

the done contract.plain: the list, agreed before building starts, of what must be true for the work to count as finished; it is turned into tests before any code is written
the done contract.phrase: the agreed list of what counts as finished
the done contract.example: Like the checklist a builder and owner sign before the handover walk-through.
